answer.rationale:
memory_c2 is the memory that would license the tempting move (full switch to the low-cost vendor, which alone satisfies the 18% mandate), so it is the one worth the single verification pull. As consolidated, c2 records only unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy 	ime-in-full performance at committed volume, quality escapes, capacity headroom, or whether the part was this constrained/critical component. Those are exactly the dimensions that matter when the line runs at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and the contract lapses in 14 days with no auto-renew. A cost-and-invoicing success record is not evidence of delivery reliability; treating it as such would trade a measurable cost win for an unmeasured continuity exposure, and the stated objective forbids increasing delivery risk.

Given one decision this cycle, I intend to negotiate terms rather than switch. The incumbent has refused to reopen price this cycle, but c4 shows benchmarking has moved them on both price and payment terms before, and c6 shows multi-year commitment structure unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope \low low-cost vendor's quote is real leverage even if I never execute against it, and term/payment-term/multi-year levers are a different door than the one the incumbent just closed. c1 supports that continuity with the incumbent is the low-risk baseline while the line has no buffer. I hold this guarded: I do not assume negotiation reaches the full 18%, and I am not concluding the low-cost vendor is unfit enegotc2 verification shows delivery and quality performance at comparable volume, the right next-cycle move is qualifying them as a second source (c3) and shifting volume gradually rather than a cliff-edge primary switch 14 days out. If negotiation lands short of the mandate, the gap should be escalated to finance as a scope/timing question rather than closed by accepting unquantified supply risk.
